The ancient city of Ur in southern Iraq contained a cemetery excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s–1930s with over 1,840 graves; 16 of them were 'Royal Tombs' with multiple human burials showing that attendants and guards died alongside the primary occupant; a 2009 CT analysis of one royal tomb's skeletal attendants showed bone remodelling consistent with long-term servitude and malnutrition, suggesting the sacrificed individuals were long-serving household members rather than freshly captured strangers.

The 2020 paper by Dalya Abramovich identifying a 5,000-year-old pottery kiln at Horvat Beter, Israel, as producing Chalcolithic ceramic wares with a specific clay recipe combining local marl with volcanic temper from the Golan Heights — transported 200 km — showed that Chalcolithic potters engaged in long-distance sourcing of specific raw materials for quality control rather than using immediately available local clays; this economic complexity in raw material procurement predates the appearance of writing in the region by 500 years.

The Xiaohe (Small River) Cemetery in the Tarim Basin, Xinjiang, China — 'found' in 1934 by Folke Bergman and lost again until relocated in 2000 — contains approximately 200 mummies buried in boat-shaped coffins dated to 3,800–4,000 years ago; genetic analysis published in 2021 showed these 'Tarim Basin mummies' were an isolated Bronze Age population with no direct connection to modern East Asian, European, or South Asian populations, descended from Ancient North Eurasians who had lived in the Tarim Basin for millennia.

The pre-Columbian Puerto Rican Taino site of Tibes, near Ponce, contains the largest known ceremonial complex in the Caribbean: nine earthen plazas and two ball courts, dated to 600–900 CE, where thousands gathered for areyto ceremonies involving music, dance, and ball games; bioarchaeological analysis of 187 human burials from the site shows a population with artificially flattened frontal bones (intentional cranial modification) that served as a visual marker of Taino social identity across the island.

The Vindolanda tablet #291 — a birthday dinner invitation written by Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, wife of the fort's commander, around 100 CE — is the oldest known handwritten letter from a woman in Latin script; the final line 'I shall expect you, sister' is written in a different hand identified as Claudia Severa's own (the rest was written by a scribe), making it the oldest surviving example of writing by an identified British woman.

The Late Bronze Age city of Emar on the Euphrates (modern Tell Meskene, Syria), excavated before its submersion under Lake Assad, contained a temple archive of 1,400 cuneiform tablets recording local laws, ritual procedures, and commercial transactions; the Emar ritual texts document a unique festival called zukru in which god statues were processed around the city perimeter every seven years, and the same festival is described in Ugaritic texts 200 km away — confirming pan-Levantine shared religious practices in the Bronze Age.

source.name: Journal of the American Oriental Society

text: The Toltec city of Tula in Mexico (c. 900–1150 CE) is identified with the legendary Tollan of Aztec oral tradition — a mythical city of towers and turquoise palaces — through its monumental pyramid with four massive warrior pillars (Atlantean figures) 4.6 metres tall; the iconography of Tula warrior warriors appears identically at Chichén Itzá in Yucatán 1,600 km away, confirming that Toltec militaristic ideology spread deep into the Maya world through a poorly understood political or religious network.

The 'Ness of Brodgar' site on Orkney, excavated since 2008, has revealed the most complex Neolithic structure ever found in northern Europe: a massive walled enclosure 100 x 25 metres (Structure 10) with internal subdivisions, decorated stonework, and evidence for feasting on a scale that implies island-wide gatherings; the site's final destruction — all buildings simultaneously filled with cattle bones and tools and demolished in a single act around 2300 BCE — was the largest known deliberate destruction event in Neolithic Britain.

source.name: University of the Highlands and Islands Archaeology Institute

text: The 'Lindisfarne Gospels', written on Holy Island, Northumbria, c. 715–720 CE, is the finest example of Insular manuscript art; X-ray fluorescence mapping of the pigments has identified over 90 different pigment preparations using lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, kermes from the Mediterranean, and indigo from southern Asia — confirming that the Northumbrian monastic economy was embedded in a global trade network stretching from the Himalayas to the North Sea in the early 8th century.

Phosphate analysis of soils beneath Roman fort floors — measuring the accumulation of phosphorus compounds from human and animal waste — has allowed archaeologists to map latrine locations, animal stabling, and kitchen areas within military barracks without excavating intact floor deposits; at the Roman fort of Bremetenacum (Ribchester, Lancashire), phosphate mapping identified a previously unknown 'praetorium' (commander's house) annex that had left no visible architectural trace above the plough zone.

The ancient Maya astronomical observatory at Caracol in Belize — identified by its circular base and open-air summit — was aligned so that windows in the tower's upper section framed the rise and set of Venus at its extreme northern and southern positions; Venus observations were central to Maya warfare calendrics, and archaeological evidence shows that Caracol's military conquests, documented in hieroglyphic texts, were timed to Venus rise events as dictated by the city's astronomers.

The Khmer reservoir system at Angkor, including the Western Baray (8 x 2.1 km, capacity 53 million cubic metres), was not merely for water storage but formed part of a religious landscape centred on the concept of Mount Meru rising from a cosmic ocean; sediment coring of the barays has shown they silted up gradually from the 13th century as Angkor's population abandoned its northern agricultural suburbs, suggesting the collapse of Angkor was a slow agricultural contraction rather than a sudden catastrophe.

The Bactrian-Margiana Archaeological Complex (BMAC or 'Oxus Civilisation'), centred on modern Turkmenistan and Afghanistan (c. 2300–1700 BCE), was an urban Bronze Age culture unknown to scholarship until Soviet excavations in the 1970s; its distinctive stamp seals, chlorite vessels, and multi-room palatial compounds have now been identified across the Middle East from the Persian Gulf to the Indus, showing BMAC was a major trading culture connecting Central Asia to the entire Bronze Age world.

The Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit, founded in 1981 as the world's first commercial AMS (accelerator mass spectrometry) radiocarbon facility, demonstrated that AMS dating requires samples 1,000 times smaller than conventional radiocarbon and can date materials like single seeds, single hair fibres, and individual handwriting ink; the unit's early results included re-dating the Turin Shroud to 1260–1390 CE (1988), the oldest book of Kells vellum to the 8th century CE, and the Vindolanda tablets — all without destroying visible parts of the objects.

The Roman gladiatorial school (ludus magnus) adjacent to the Colosseum in Rome was excavated in 2011–2012 and found to contain a fully intact training arena — a small oval track surrounded by cells for individual gladiators — exactly as depicted in a wall painting from Pompeii; skeletal analysis of gladiators from a cemetery at Ephesus, Turkey, published in 2014, showed they were well-fed with a plant-based diet high in ash residues (from drinking plant ash for bone repair), contradicting the popular image of brutal mistreatment.

The 2023 Herculaneum scroll project — using X-ray phase-contrast tomography and AI-assisted virtual unwrapping at the Vesuvius Challenge — successfully deciphered portions of a 2,000-year-old carbonised papyrus scroll from the Villa dei Papiri without physically unrolling it; the decoded text was identified as a philosophical work by Philodemus of Gadara discussing pleasure, confirming that the villa's library of over 1,800 scrolls contains Epicurean philosophy texts not otherwise known to survive, potentially transforming understanding of Hellenistic philosophy.

The earliest known textile fragment in the world — a flax linen cloth from Nahal Hemar Cave in the Judean Desert, dated to approximately 6500 BCE — preserves not only weave structure but also evidence of a woven band hem decorated with a looped fringe border; the find demonstrates that Neolithic textiles were not crude burlap but included decorative embellishment comparable to modern weaving, implying an already sophisticated fibre craft tradition by the 7th millennium BCE.

The Peruvian coastal site of Caral's contemporary society, the Norte Chico civilisation, lacked writing and pottery but built 30 monumental platform mound cities simultaneously between 3000 and 1800 BCE — a social coordination achievement that challenges the assumption that writing is a prerequisite for complex society; quipu-like knotted cord records (precursors of the Inca quipu) found at Caral may have functioned as administrative accounting devices, suggesting record-keeping can precede literacy by millennia.

The 14th-century CE Black Death (Yersinia pestis pandemic) killed approximately 30–60% of Europe's population, and its mortality gradient has been studied through cemetery demography; isotopic analysis of pre- and post-plague cemetery populations from Hereford, England, shows that post-plague survivors were significantly taller on average — the 'Black Death advantage' — as reduced population pressure improved nutrition, demonstrating archaeology can document the demographic and health legacy of pandemics.

The construction of Sacsayhuamán, the massive Inca stone fortress above Cusco built between approximately 1438 and 1471 CE, required moving 3-tonne to 360-tonne stones from quarries up to 32 km away across the Andes; experimental archaeology using Peruvian volunteers has demonstrated that a single 2-tonne stone can be moved 100 metres per day using wooden sledges, ropes, and levers by 24 people, implying that the 30,000-person workforce described in Spanish documents could have built Sacsayhuamán in the approximately 70 years documented.

The Nihewan Basin in Hebei Province, China, contains the earliest evidence for hominin occupation of East Asia at approximately 1.66 million years ago — the Majuangou III site; associated Oldowan-style stone tools and faunal remains of extinct rhinos, deer, and horses suggest that hominins reached China from Africa within a few hundred thousand years of their initial expansion — a migration timeline so rapid it implies sustained, directed movement through continental Asia rather than diffuse, random dispersal.

The Denisova Cave in the Altai Mountains has served as a hominin residence for at least 300,000 years, as shown by the presence of Neanderthal, Denisovan, and modern human occupations in successive layers; the cave's sedaDNA — environmental DNA extracted from the cave sediment itself without any skeletal material — has been shown to preserve hominin DNA dating back 200,000 years, meaning the Denisova Cave sediment archive may contain genetic evidence of hominin visits too brief to have left skeletal material.

The Maya city of Quiriguá in Guatemala has the tallest freestanding carved stone monuments in the pre-Columbian world — the stelae, carved between 720 and 810 CE, include Stela E at 10.67 metres and weighing 65 tonnes, covered on all four faces with hieroglyphic inscriptions recording the deeds of ruler K'ahk' Tiliw Chan Yopaat; the inscriptions document his defeat and ritual decapitation of Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil of Copán, a military upset that shocked the Maya world.

The Roman town of Timgad (Thamugadi) in Algeria, founded in 100 CE as a military colony, has its entire cardo (north-south main street) and decumanus (east-west main street) intersection preserved in perfect condition under desert sand; photogrammetric mapping of the site in 2015 created a sub-millimetre resolution 3D model of the entire 50-hectare town that allowed digital reconstruction of all standing walls and is now used as the primary training dataset for AI-assisted Roman town analysis.

The Peiligang culture of central China (c. 7000–5000 BCE) represents the earliest known settled agricultural society in East Asia, with millet farming, pig and dog domestication, and a distinctive jadeite bracelet tradition; bone flutes from Jiahu — the same site that produced the world's oldest fermented beverage evidence — include a 9,000-year-old crane-bone flute that can still play all seven notes of the pentatonic scale, making it the oldest playable musical instrument yet discovered.

The West Kennet long barrow in Wiltshire, England — a 100-metre-long Neolithic megalithic tomb dated to approximately 3600–3400 BCE — was used for communal burial over at least 1,000 years, with the remains of at least 46 individuals deposited in its five chambers; micro-CT scanning of the skeletal assemblage in 2016 showed many bones had been deliberately rearranged, sorted by type, and mixed across generations, suggesting a Neolithic practice of periodic reordering of the dead as an ongoing ritual rather than simple successive inhumation.

The Keatley Creek housepit village in British Columbia, occupied by ancestral Stl'atl'imx (Lillooet) people between approximately 1500 BCE and 1400 CE, contains the largest pithouse (Feature 3, c. 18 metres in diameter) in the Canadian interior; zooarchaeological analysis of salmon vertebrae in the refuse deposits has quantified the number of salmon smoked per household per year — an estimated 35,000 fish — demonstrating that Interior Plateau peoples had developed a complex salmon storage and redistribution economy without agriculture.

The Hierakonpolis Predynastic Egyptian site (c. 3500–3100 BCE), excavated since 1978 by Renée Friedman, has produced the earliest-known Egyptian royal cemetery with individual tombs showing deliberate human sacrifice; a tomb of 3500 BCE had five subsidiary burials of young adult males with cervical dislocations consistent with strangulation or decapitation — predating the First Dynasty royal sacrifices at Abydos by 400 years and extending the roots of Egyptian royal ideology back into the Predynastic period.

The 'Nile Meter' (Nilometer) on Rhoda Island in Cairo, constructed in 861 CE and still standing, is the oldest functioning hydrological instrument in the world; it measures the annual Nile flood levels on a graduated column, and records of flood levels have been kept continuously since at least 622 CE — giving a 1,400-year hydrological time series that is one of the oldest instrumental environmental records in existence, used by climatologists to study historical drought and flood cycles in northeast Africa.

The Sican (Lambayeque) culture burial discovered at Huaca Loro, Peru, in 1991 by Izumi Shimada was the richest unlooted South American burial found in the 20th century: a tomb containing a single individual — identified as a Middle Sican (c. 950–1100 CE) lord — interred upside-down in a seated foetal position, surrounded by 1.2 tonnes of gold and silver objects, 500 kg of smashed ceramics, and at least 11 sacrificed retainers wrapped in textiles.

The Tepe Hissar site in Iran, excavated in the 1930s and reanalysed since 2009, contains the largest Bronze Age copper hoard from Iran — 433 copper objects including axes, chisels, and pins dated to c. 2500–2000 BCE; metallurgical analysis shows that the copper was smelted with natural arsenical copper ore rather than intentional tin bronze, and the arsenic content follows a precise quality gradient from implements (high arsenic, hard) to ornamental pins (low arsenic, soft), demonstrating deliberate quality-controlled Bronze Age metallurgy.

The Alley of Sphinxes at Luxor, Egypt — a 3-km ceremonial processional road lined with 1,350 stone sphinxes connecting Karnak Temple to Luxor Temple — was substantially excavated and restored between 2005 and 2021; analysis of the construction phases showed the avenue was built by at least six different pharaohs over 1,600 years, with each ruler adding their own sphinxes in slightly different styles while maintaining the avenue's overall design, making it the longest-running single architectural project in Egyptian history.

The Cochno Stone in West Dunbartonshire, Scotland, bears 90 cup-and-ring marks in concentric circles with radial grooves, the most complex example of prehistoric rock art in Britain; experimental photogrammetry and structure-from-motion modelling conducted during its 2016 re-exposure produced a digital model showing that many rings are not visible from standing height but only when viewed at oblique angles, suggesting the rock art was designed to be experienced while crawling or kneeling — a ritual posture of supplication.

The Kerch Straits underwater survey (Crimea) has mapped over 50 ancient shipwrecks from the 5th century BCE to the 13th century CE on a seabed stretch between the Black Sea and Sea of Azov; one Hellenistic wreck contains intact amphora stacks from six different production centres simultaneously, documenting the Black Sea wine trade at a moment of maximum commercial diversity; another Byzantine wreck has over 700 intact ceramic lamps in crates, the largest consignment of ancient lamps ever found in situ.

Experimental use-wear analysis — examining microscopic edge damage on replicated stone tools after use on different materials — has been used since the 1970s to identify the function of ancient stone tools without removing them from archives; a comprehensive 2019 meta-analysis of 44 published use-wear studies found that the method can reliably distinguish butchery, hide-working, wood-working, and plant-processing tools with 85–95% accuracy when performed by experienced analysts, making use-wear one of the most productive functional analysis methods in lithic studies.
